rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the six-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

The first method already achieves the maximum CRF. Shortening only the gradient tests whether we can retain full resolution while reducing the last-peak time, using the current minimum resolution of 2.68 as a margin.
Test the next shorter gradient to locate the full-resolution speed limit at 40 C. Injection 2 remains a maximum-CRF fallback if the slope-sensitive central pair drops below 1.5.

Test whether higher temperature restores selectivity for the central pair at the shorter gradient while further reducing retention. Injection 2 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested, already achieving maximum CRF.

Test the lower temperature limit at the six-minute gradient to seek improved central-pair selectivity without the early-pair coelution seen at 60 C. This isolates temperature effects while retaining injection 2 as a maximum-CRF fallback.

Use a shallower six-minute gradient to improve the slope-sensitive central pair, with an intermediate temperature to avoid the early-pair collapse at 60 C. The reduced endpoint remains well above the observed elution window and could yield full resolution faster than injection 2.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving the slope of injection 6 to remove some low-organic delay. This tests a shorter fully resolved separation while monitoring both the early pair and the central pair, whose resolution margin is small.

Raise the starting organic fraction to reduce initial delay, but make the gradient slightly shallower to protect the central pair’s narrow resolution margin. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction of 0.51, making this a promising shorter, fully resolved method.

Shift the successful four-minute gradient upward by 0.05 at unchanged slope and temperature to shorten retention further. Monitor the early pair for compression and the central pair for loss of its current 1.79 resolution.

Reduce the gradient slope one grid step to restore the central pair, which narrowly missed full resolution in injection 9. Retaining the higher starting organic fraction should keep this faster than injection 8 while recovering maximum CRF.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step while keeping the endpoint fixed, combining less initial delay with a shallower gradient to protect the central pair. This tests whether the early pair remains resolved as its retention approaches the unretained region.

Explore a much steeper gradient at low temperature to test whether the central pair separates again after an elution-order crossover. This is a distinct route to a faster maximum-CRF method, with injection 11 retained as the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Test a higher starting organic fraction at low temperature to seek useful selectivity on the opposite side of the central-pair crossover. Lower temperature may preserve early-pair retention while the shifted, shallower gradient separates the central pair.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction strengthens separation after the central-pair order reversal, with a shallower slope to limit compression. This explores a different selectivity region while preserving injection 11 as a maximum-CRF fallback.

Shorten injection 14’s gradient to test slope sensitivity in the reversed central-pair region. A steeper gradient may improve that pair’s selectivity while bringing the last peak out sooner; the early pair currently has resolution margin.

The central pair barely responded to gradient duration, so test a higher starting organic fraction instead while preserving injection 15’s slope. This may improve central-pair selectivity, although compression of the early pair is the main risk.

Test temperature selectivity at injection 15’s fast gradient, where only the central pair missed full resolution. A five-degree change isolates whether that pair can reach 1.5 while retaining the early pair’s resolution margin.

Return to the fastest fully resolved method and test a five-degree temperature decrease to measure local selectivity. This will show whether improved early-pair separation can support further window adjustment without sacrificing the central pair.

Test whether a five-degree increase restores the central pair that narrowly failed in injection 9 while shortening its 3.37-minute last-peak time. The early pair is the main risk, so retain injection 11 as the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Test a two-minute gradient with a shallower slope to protect the central pair, followed by a hold that may elute the final compounds promptly. This explores a shorter programmed gradient while retaining injection 11 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved separation.

Raise the endpoint one step to shorten the final peak’s hold-period retention from injection 20. This tests whether the central pair can tolerate the steeper two-minute gradient while preserving maximum CRF.

Use the six-minute grid to obtain a slope between injections 9 and 10, targeting full central-pair resolution with less retention than injection 10. This refines the fast, maximum-CRF region without pushing the early peaks closer to the dead time.

Slightly steepen injection 11’s gradient using the finer slope increment available with six minutes. This targets a last-peak time below 3.40 minutes while testing the central pair’s remaining resolution margin.

Test a higher starting fraction with a shallower gradient to offset the central-pair resolution loss seen when shifting the window upward. Using 45 C should provide more early-pair separation than 50 C, potentially opening a neighboring fully resolved operating region.

Use the final injection to improve resolution margin around injection 11 by reducing its endpoint one step. This preserves the successful initial slope of injection 20 but continues the gradient beyond 0.40 to avoid its slow final-peak hold elution, targeting a robust maximum-CRF alternative.
